claude-code-setup.what_it_does:
It is one model-invocable skill, "claude-automation-recommender". Nothing runs in the background: no hooks, MCP server, daemon or proxy.
- **Every session (and every subagent, since this subagent's own listing includes it):** only the skill's name and description (354 characters) sit in the skill listing. The full SKILL.md loads only when Claude decides the description matches the request or the user invokes it. The description says to trigger on "optimize their Claude Code setup", "improving Claude Code workflows", "what Claude Code features they should use", and similar.
- **When invoked:**
  - Phase 1: Claude runs Read/Glob/Grep/Bash discovery (ls package.json/pyproject/Cargo, cat package.json, ls .claude/ CLAUDE.md, ls src/ tests/ ...).
  - Phase 2: it maps what it finds to recommendations from its reference tables. These cover MCP servers (context7, Playwright, GitHub, Linear, Sentry, Supabase/Convex, "Memory MCP"), skills, hooks (formatter, linter, type-check or run tests on PostToolUse; block .env/lock-file edits; Notification sounds), subagents (code-reviewer, security-reviewer, test-writer, ...) and plugins (hookify, commit-commands, pr-review-toolkit, LSP plugins). It is told to "use web search" to go beyond the lists.
  - Phase 3: it prints a markdown report with 1-2 items per category and offers to implement them.
- **Does it write files or settings?** The SKILL.md and README both say "This skill is read-only ... It does NOT create or modify any files." That is only an instruction in prose. The frontmatter field it uses, "tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash", is not a SKILL.md field in the official docs (code.claude.com/docs/en/skills lists allowed-tools/disallowed-tools; there is no "tools" field), so nothing restricts tools. It does not pre-approve anything either: there is no allowed-tools field. With the user's permissions.defaultMode=auto, any follow-up ("help me set up X") would go through the normal auto-mode classifier. The report it produces ends by offering to install MCP servers (for example `claude mcp add context7`), create .claude/settings.json hooks, and install plugins.

Across a large Ultracode workflow, for example 30 subagents, that is a few thousand tokens. - **Net for this user:** a small negative standing cost and no ongoing benefit. It is worth it only as a one-off, explicitly invoked run.

freellmapi.what_it_does:
A self-hosted Express proxy (Node 20+, Docker image ghcr.io/tashfeenahmed/freellmapi:latest, or a desktop tray app) listens on localhost:3001. It exposes OpenAI-style endpoints (/v1/chat/completions, /responses, /completions, /embeddings, images, video, audio), an Anthropic Messages surface (/v1/messages, count_tokens), a native Gemini /v1beta surface, opt-in Ollama emulation, and an optional MCP server at /mcp.

For each request a router picks a model:
- It ranks models with a Thompson-sampling bandit over reliability, speed and intelligence.
- It enforces per-key RPM/RPD/TPM/TPD limits in a SQLite ledger.
- On 429/5xx it fails over across up to 20 attempts, possibly switching to a different model and provider mid-conversation. Conversations are "sticky" to one model for 30 minutes.

Access to upstreams uses provider API keys (mostly official free tiers, which you sign up for yourself), stored AES-256-GCM-encrypted in SQLite. Some providers are registered "keyless" and auto-configure with no key at all:
- AI Horde: volunteer-run workers, anonymous key 0000000000.
- Kilo Gateway: the source comment says "Free prompts/outputs are logged for training".
- OVH AI Endpoints: anonymous mode.

The provider list includes Google AI Studio, Groq, Cerebras, Mistral, OpenRouter, Cloudflare, Cohere, NVIDIA NIM, HuggingFace, Z.ai/Zhipu, ModelScope, Ollama Cloud, OpenCode Zen and LLM7. It also includes many third-party relay or reseller gateways: Api.Airforce, ElectronHub, Router9, LLMTR, free.ai, IteraCompute, Apinex, BlockRun, Pollinations and others (directory server/src/providers/).

I found no scraping or reuse of web-chat sessions in the code I read. However, several relays are opaque intermediaries whose own upstream access I could not verify. The code itself guards against Airforce returning "a different or missing model identity" and against ElectronHub "proxy error" bodies that "may contain provider credential details".

Background activity:
- It syncs an Ed25519-signed model catalog from https://api.freellmapi.co twice a day. Free installs get a 30-day-delayed snapshot; Premium installs send their fla_ license key as a Bearer token. The catalog can add or remove model rows on registered platforms without user action.
- It runs periodic key health probes.
- It keeps request analytics (90 days by default), server logs (7 days) and decision logs (90 days).

Optional features:
- Prompt compression: off by default; lossless / standard / aggressive modes.
- A response cache.
- Context handoff: it injects a system message with a recent-session summary when the model switches.
- "Fusion": fans one prompt out to several models in parallel.

For Claude Code you set ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:3001 and ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=freellmapi-..., or run `npx freellmapi setup-claude`, which merges into the Claude config with a backup. `npx freellmapi launch` keeps credentials off disk. The Claude families default/opus/sonnet/haiku all map to "auto", meaning the free pool, by default (server/src/services/anthropic-map.ts DEFAULT_MAP). The installer is `curl | bash` and pulls :latest.
freellmapi.token_effect:
Claimed: "7.4 billion tokens per month, 34 providers, 635 free endpoints" (README, catalog as of 2026-10). This is a plain sum of every provider's listed free-tier allowance, assuming you have an account and key on all 34. It is not one pool and not a measured throughput. Independent write-ups note the per-day caps bind long before any monthly total (buildmvpfast.com review; the project's own Limitations section). The project's own docs say "Intelligence degrades as the day progresses": the top models (Gemini Flash, DeepSeek V4, Kimi) have the smallest daily caps, after which the router falls to "smaller/weaker models" until UTC midnight. Frontier-class rows exist but have "the smallest daily allowances, the longest queues".

FreeLLMAPI does not save Claude tokens. It replaces Claude: every turn of a Claude Code session pointed at it goes to free third-party models, and Opus 5.5 is never called. The only real "saving" is that such sessions use no Anthropic plan quota.

The opt-in compression's "saved~=N" figures are chars/4 estimates, not measured. Its standard and aggressive modes filter tool output, drop stale file reads, condense older turns and filter by lexical relevance. They are lossy by design, though a fidelity gate keeps numeric literals, diffs and error lines.

Extra costs: Fusion multiplies calls per prompt; failover retries spend quota on several providers; context handoff adds a system message.

For this user's workload, a C11 allocator with a signal-safety thesis, security review findings, and benchmark numbers that must be exact:
- Quality loss is severe.
- The model can change silently mid-task (X-Routed-Via is a response header Claude Code does not show).
- Small-context models get the requests after compression trims them.
- Tool-call "rescue" turns plain-text tool calls from weaker models into real tool_calls, a known source of wrong edits.
- There is no extended thinking or effort "max" equivalent.
- Ultracode workflows fan out many subagents; each would hit rate limits at once and land on the weakest healthy model.

Expected net effect: zero Anthropic quota for routed sessions at a large, unpredictable drop in correctness, plus wasted human review time. It is not a sensible answer to the usage-limit problem for this research.
freellmapi.research_reliability:
High risk on every axis the task names:
- Model routing: Claude Code's "opus" maps to "auto", so a random free model, which changes with quota state and time of day, writes the code and analysis.
- Mid-session failover: the model can switch without any notice in the Claude Code UI.
- Context handoff (opt-in): injects a synthetic system message with a summary of recent turns.
- Prompt compression (opt-in): standard and aggressive modes delete or condense earlier tool output, file reads and turns, so the model may not see the exact benchmark output or reproducer text it is asked about. Lossless mode is safer, but it still rewrites JSON into tables.
- Fusion: synthesizes one answer from several models' drafts through a judge model, which can blend or fabricate.
- Response cache (opt-in): can replay a stored answer.
- Relay providers: the codebase itself contains checks for relays returning a different model than requested (Api.Airforce) and HTTP-200 bodies that are really proxy errors (ElectronHub). In other words, response identity and integrity from some upstreams are not assured.

Weaker free models are much more likely to misquote numbers, invent citations, or "summarize" raw benchmark tables incorrectly. That conflicts directly with the project's evidence rules. Anything produced this way would have to be re-verified, and the research log would have to record which model (X-Routed-Via) produced each claim. FreeLLMAPI does not write to Claude Code's auto-memory directly, but anything a degraded model writes into memory files or docs/STATUS.md would persist into later sessions.
freellmapi.security:
Data flow if used with Claude Code: the full request context leaves the machine on every turn. That includes the system prompt, CLAUDE.md and auto-memory contents, every file Claude reads (allocator source, docs/research-log/data/* review findings and reproducers, bench/out/* raw results), tool outputs and diffs. It goes to whichever upstream the router picks, which can differ per request.

Upstream data handling (verified):
- Google Gemini API unpaid tier: Google "uses the content you submit ... and any generated responses to provide, improve, and develop Google products ... and machine learning technologies"; "human reviewers may read, annotate, and process your API input and output"; "Do not submit sensitive, confidential, or personal information to the Unpaid Services" (https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/terms).
- Kilo Gateway: source comment says "Free prompts/outputs are logged for training" (server/src/providers/index.ts).
- OpenCode Zen free models: "prompts/outputs may be used to improve the models" (same file).
- AI Horde: inference runs on anonymous volunteer workers, so any third party running a worker can see prompts. It is registered keyless and "auto-configures and works anonymously".
- Relay resellers (Airforce, ElectronHub, Router9, LLMTR, free.ai, IteraCompute, etc.): unknown operators, logging and jurisdictions.
- Z.ai/Zhipu and ModelScope are Chinese/Singapore entities.

All of these are outside the stated trust boundary ("public paste services and third-party clouds are outside it"). The keyless providers mean a fresh install can route prompts to such endpoints before you add a single key.

Network endpoints:
- localhost:3001 (Docker installer binds 127.0.0.1 by default; HOST_BIND=0.0.0.0 exposes it to the LAN; the docs say "don't expose it to the internet").
- Desktop dashboard 127.0.0.1:31415 with automatic sign-in.
- Optional /mcp endpoint.
- Optional ChatGPT Secure MCP Tunnel through OpenAI.
- The catalog service api.freellmapi.co (twice daily; sends the Premium license key when set). The README says it "never sees your prompts, completions, or provider keys". I did not audit that beyond catalog-sync.ts's fetch calls, which send only the license header.

Credentials: provider keys are encrypted at rest with an ENCRYPTION_KEY kept in .env. The unified key is a bearer token. URL tokens can be issued for headerless clients.

Supply chain: a single maintainer plus 98 contributors and AI-assisted commits; daily commits. `curl | bash` installer; Docker image pinned to :latest; desktop auto-update via electron latest-*.yml. A remotely updated signed catalog changes which upstream models get traffic without a code update.

Terms of service, from the project's own May 2026 review (docs/en/architecture/00-high-level-index.md):
- Cohere: "Avoid" (forbids personal use).
- Google: "Caution" (2026 terms limit use to "professional or business purposes").
- NVIDIA NIM: "evaluation only, not production".
- Z.ai: an anti-traffic-redirect clause.
- Gemini terms also bar sending confidential data on the unpaid tier.
- Relay resellers' own right to resell the models they serve is unverified.

Anthropic side: pointing ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL at a gateway is a documented configuration and not a terms violation in itself. But it disables Remote Control, and none of the traffic goes to Anthropic.
freellmapi.overlap:
It would take over the role of the Anthropic backend entirely. That conflicts with the core setup (Opus 5.5 at max, Ultracode, Remote Control) rather than adding to it.

Overlap with other evaluated tools:
- Prompt compression overlaps the headroom MCP server (headroom-ai 0.41.0) and claude-mem's context features. Stacking several compression layers makes it harder to know what the model actually saw.
- The response cache and context handoff overlap claude-mem's memory injection.
- Its MCP server would add another set of tools to the session.
- claude-mem is set to CLAUDE_MEM_PROVIDER=claude with Haiku. Pointing that, or Hermes Agent, at FreeLLMAPI would send every captured tool event to free upstreams, a worse leak than the main session.
- Its `setup-claude`, `setup-hermes` and other generators edit agent configs, which would collide with the user's managed ~/.claude settings.

Unlike claude-mem or headroom, it does not hook Claude Code events. It works only through ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL or ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, so the conflict is total but easy to see.
freellmapi.compatibility:
Opus 5.5 max: incompatible in practice. With ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL set to FreeLLMAPI, Claude Code's model names, including opus, are mapped to the free pool ("auto" by default, or a pinned free model or tier). Opus 5.5 is never reached, and the "max" reasoning effort has no equivalent; pass-through of thinking parameters to free models is unverified.

Ultracode / Workflow subagents: technically they would run, since every subagent call goes through the same base URL. But each subagent multiplies requests against tight per-provider RPM/RPD caps. That causes 429 storms, failover onto the weakest models and wildly varying latency (the docs: "Latency is highly variable", "No SLA, by definition"). FreeLLMAPI installs no Claude Code hooks, so it has no per-subagent hook cost; the cost is quality and quota exhaustion.

Remote Control: incompatible, verified. The Claude Code docs say Remote Control is "not available" when "You point ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL at a host other than api.anthropic.com, such as an LLM gateway or proxy. omniroute.what_it_does:
OmniRoute is a local HTTP gateway and proxy, not a Claude Code plugin. It has no hooks, skills or plugin manifest for Claude Code.
- Server: `omniroute` starts a Next.js standalone server on port 20128 (dashboard plus OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible /v1 inference endpoints), a supervisor and many background schedulers. Defaults: model sync every 6h, provider limits every 70m, credential health hourly, token auto-refresh every 15 min, Arena ELO and OpenRouter stats daily, cleanup every 6h.
- Claude Code integration works by overriding ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL (http://localhost:20128, no /v1) and ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN (an OmniRoute API key). `omniroute launch` injects both into a spawned `claude` process. `omniroute setup-claude` writes one ~/.claude/profiles/<name>/settings.json per model, setting ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL and ANTHROPIC_MODEL, for use with CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR (bin/cli/commands/setup-claude.mjs; maintainer answer in GitHub discussion #11127).
- Every Claude Code request then goes to OmniRoute. It translates the request formats and sends it to whichever upstream "provider" or "combo" (fallback chain) is configured. The catalog claims 375 providers and 1,400+ models (Claude, GPT, Gemini, Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek, Qwen, ...), with 20 routing strategies and quota-aware auto-fallback.
- Ways it reaches providers: API keys, OAuth logins that reuse the official CLIs' OAuth clients (including a "claude" provider), web-session/cookie impersonation providers, and "CLI fingerprint" plus browser-like TLS fingerprint spoofing (SECURITY.md, docs/security/STEALTH_GUIDE.md).
- Request pipeline: authz, guardrails (PII masker, prompt-injection heuristics, vision bridge), "RTK + Caveman" stacked token compression of tool output, semantic cache, rate limiter and circuit breaker, then the provider.
- Also bundled: its own memory store, MCP server, A2A/ACP agents, a "headroom" integration, cloud sync (CLOUD_URL), cloudflared/ngrok/tailscale tunnels, and a MITM component under src/mitm (certificate install, DNS, tproxy, sudo gate) used for some IDE integrations. It also checks npm for updates daily.

omniroute.research_reliability:
HIGH RISK to research reliability, in four ways.
1. Model substitution. Combos and auto-fallback can silently serve a request from a different model (e.g. the README's examples cc/claude-opus → nvidia/llama-3.3-70b → glm-4.7 → kimi-k2-thinking). Claude Code would still believe it is talking to the configured model, so results attributed to "Opus 5.5 max" could come from other models, inconsistently across subagents.
2. Compression. RTK and Caveman are lossy rewrites of tool results and context. Per-key compressionEnabled is true for the self-loop key in src/lib/db/apiKeys.ts; whether the global default is on is unverified. This can drop or alter exact benchmark numbers, log lines, reproducer output and quotes before the model reads them, which is exactly the evidence this project depends on.
3. Its own semantic cache, memory store and guardrails rewrite requests. The PII masker rewrites things like emails and phone patterns, and the prompt-injection heuristics can block "high" severity matches (SECURITY.md). Security-testing text, such as review findings that quote attack strings, can trigger false positives.
4. Translating the reasoning/effort and thinking parameters for non-Anthropic upstreams cannot preserve Opus "max" effort semantics. Even with an Anthropic upstream, pass-through fidelity is unverified.

task-observer.what_it_does:
(A) is a skill only: instruction text plus bash and Python helpers. It has no hooks, no MCP server, no daemon and no network code. Everything runs because the model follows the text.

How it triggers:
- Its 1,001-character description sits in the skill listing of every session and every subagent. It says: "IMPORTANT: invoke this skill before the FIRST tool call of any session and before writing or proposing a plan — any turn that will involve a tool call counts."
- It also triggers on "ANY multi-step task, agentic workflow, or work session".

Once invoked, it runs a Session Start Protocol:
1. Probes or creates a workspace at a pinned absolute path. For a Claude Code user-scope skill it recommends ~/.claude/skill-observations/, or ~/.claude/projects/<id>/. It explicitly says never use the working directory or a worktree.
2. Creates skill-observations/ (observation-log/ with archive/ and .id-floor, last-review-date.txt, checkpoints.log, starter-principles-reviewed.txt) and later skill-updates/ with PENDING.md.
3. Offers to import "starter principles", once.
4. Scans the frontmatter of every observation.
5. Offers a review once per session if the last review is 7 or more days old.
6. Suggests adding an activation block to CLAUDE.md.
7. Offers a "first-run backfill" that mines the project's own history (handover and decision docs, commit history, test scripts, notes or memory directories, CLAUDE.md) into observations.

During work it:
- writes one NNNN-slug.md per observation (Issue / Improvement / Principle, YAML frontmatter) through scripts/new-observation.sh;
- forces a disk write after every 3rd completed todo (an observation, or a "no observations" line in checkpoints.log);
- flushes at every deliverable and after any failed external write;
- runs a grep plus a checkpoint line (skill-load.sh) every time any other skill loads;
- logs the agent's own rule violations;
- ends each task with a per-task summary of what it logged.

The weekly review (references/weekly-review.md):
- Cross-checks open observations against all installed skills and applies improvements to staged copies under [workspace]/skill-updates/<date>/. It never edits live skills; the user installs a staged copy by hand.
- Interactive mode waits for blanket or per-item approval.
- In "scheduled autonomous" mode, which it calls preferred, it applies every non-escalated observation to staged copies with nobody present. It escalates only new skills, agent-proposed removals or restructures, items it is unsure about, and conflicts.
- Step 0 recommends registering a recurring scheduler (cron or the platform's scheduled tasks) to run it.
- So it does not edit live skills automatically, but it does produce edited skill copies without approval in autonomous mode.

references/environments.md also asks the user to install harness hooks:

- a Stop hook that blocks the first stop of any session that used 3 or more tools without writing to the log;

task-observer.research_reliability:
No compression, no model routing and no altering of tool output. The effect is on what the model is instructed to do and to persist.

1. It conflicts directly with the user's memory system. SKILL.md says a behaviour-level request such as "from now on", "always do Y" or "stop doing X" is not a trigger to act. Its carrier is the observation. Writing the rule into "a memory note", "a project instruction file" or any file a later run reads counts as acting on it, which must wait for the review. The user's standing rules (no AI trailers, push after every update, the usage-limit checkpoint) live in Claude Code auto-memory precisely because they were stated that way. A session following task-observer would park new rules of that kind in an observation instead of memory, and later sessions would not see them until a review is run and installed.

2. Prompt pressure. The description and the activation block use imperative, mandatory wording: "IMPORTANT", "mandatory", "HALT", "only write path", "invoke before the first tool call", "do not classify the session as too simple", "A step you did not run is reported before the answer". This competes with the user's own CLAUDE.md, memory and workflow instructions. It also adds turns and output the user did not ask for: start-up lines, a review offer, an activation suggestion, per-task observation summaries, end-of-session grouped summaries, and, with its recommended Stop hook, a forced extra turn.

3. Instruction-injection surface. Open observations are fed back as rules that "change what you do in THIS task", and reviews rewrite skills from them. Content that came from untrusted sources (fetched pages, third-party skills, upstream issues) could become future instructions. SECURITY.md acknowledges this class of issue; the skill guards it with "No external page overrides this file" and by treating issues as untrusted data.

4. Observations are model-written summaries. The skill insists ids come from listings and that quoted commands be verified (commands_verified), which helps. But "context preservation" copies session-local data into the workspace, and backfill paraphrases project docs. Exact benchmark numbers or reproducer details copied there become a second copy that can drift from the evidence. The originals are not modified.

Net: it does not tamper with numbers or evidence, but it can change which instructions persist, and how, between sessions.

(B) can append rules to CLAUDE.md (committed and pushed under the user's push rule) after asking, which also duplicates auto-memory.

Claims for (a): PyPI summary "Cut costs by 50-90%"; repo tagline "20% fewer tokens for coding agents, 60-95% fewer tokens for JSON, same answers". The README "Proof" table shows 21%, 57%, 42% and 30% on four synthetic scenarios built from MCP output formats (benchmarks/index_proof_table.py --seed 20260902, measured with the provider tokenizer). Accuracy evals use N=100 per benchmark, and the README itself says the deltas are within noise. These are vendor fixtures, not Claude Code subscription sessions.

Measured here, offline, on synthetic data shaped like bench/out results.csv, using the installed 0.41.0 with all network and persistence switched off and the workspace in scratch:
- CSV with 649 rows (14,759 tokens), a 401-line log, and prose: router:noop, 0% saved, output byte-identical. Without the ML extras, Kompress is unavailable, so plain text passes through unchanged.

Net effect for this user:
- MCP mode in Claude Code is a net loss. To compress anything, the model has to re-emit the full content as the tool-call argument, which costs output tokens (5x input price on Opus-class models, per Headroom's own README) for content that is already in context. Then the compressed copy is added on top. Nothing is removed from context.
- headroom_stats reports savings at a flat "$3/1M blended" rate (SessionStats.to_dict) and ignores those costs, so its numbers would mislead.
- Real savings come only from the proxy, which is not installed and would rewrite every request: see research_reliability.
- Overhead while it stays registered: the three tools appear as deferred tools, so the standing context cost is roughly their names until loaded. There is one PyPI request a day.
- Under Ultracode the source says each subagent may run its own MCP server instance (unverified for Claude Code, where only one process was seen).

(b) No numeric claim. It saves tokens only to the extent Claude would otherwise read a whole large file, and it adds a short script output per file. Claude Code's built-in Read offset/limit, Grep and Bash already do the same, so the effect is small and positive for big logs, CSVs and JSON.
headroom.research_reliability:
(a) It is built to change what the model sees: compressed text replaces the original in context.
- In this install, MCP compress is a no-op for text, CSV and logs. JSON arrays become a sorted-key columnar text form whose values were exact in my tests.
- Lossy paths exist in the same code. SmartCrusher has a row-drop path that appends a {"_ccr_dropped": "<<ccr:HASH N_rows_offloaded>>"} sentinel (transforms/smart_crusher.py). Kompress ML keeps about 15% of text by default (CompressConfig.target_ratio docs). It is enabled by installing [ml]/[all] (the README's recommended `uv tool install "headroom-ai[all]"`) or by setting HEADROOM_KOMPRESS_ENDPOINT, which sends the content to a remote endpoint.
- Retrieval is by hash and expires: 1 h for MCP entries, 1800 s by default for proxy entries. After that the model is told to re-read the source.
- The proxy and wrap modes go much further. They rewrite tool outputs in every request, append "be terse" steering to the system prompt, lower thinking effort on "routine" turns (output_shaper, off by default), can inject cross-agent memory, and offer opt-in model routing. Any of these could silently alter exact benchmark numbers, sanitizer traces and reproducer output in the model's view, and degrade max-effort reasoning.
- For the sohamalloc evidence rules: never let a compressed view be the basis for a quoted number or a finding. If it is used at all, re-verify against the raw file.

claude-mem 15.0.1 (hooks/hooks.json; behaviour read from the bundled scripts/*.cjs):

- SessionStart:
  - `claude-mem start` (async) starts the worker.
  - `claude-mem hook claude-code context` (sync, 60 s timeout) injects up to CONTEXT_OBSERVATIONS=50 observations, 10 session summaries, the last summary and terminal output, plus a "# claude-mem memory use" instruction block. That block tells the model to use save_memory, search/timeline/get_observations, and work_state_write for to-do lists.
  - On startup, ensure-launcher.cjs (node, 180 s timeout) compiles the launcher with `bun build --compile` into ~/.local/bin and appends `export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"` to the shell rc file. When Bun is missing, it prints a systemMessage instead: "claude-mem: memory hooks are not active: Bun was not found... Fix: run `npx claude-mem install`".
- UserPromptSubmit (sync, 15 s): session-init records the user's prompt. It can return additionalContext (memory instructions and memory-search results).
- PreToolUse on Read|Bash|Grep|Glob|memory_search (sync, 15 s): file-context. For files of 1,500 bytes or more that have past observations, it injects a timeline of those observations as additionalContext. With FILE_READ_GATE_ENABLED=true, in the main agent only (agentId unset), it DENIES a full Read (offset ≤1 and no limit) of a code file of 32 KiB or more that has prior observations. Code means .c/.h/.py/.sh and similar; markdown, yaml, toml and unknown types are exempt. The deny reason tells the model to use smart_outline/smart_unfold or get_observations instead. In this repo that would hit src/api.c (44,987 B), src/heap.c (38,722 B) and tests/data/bigger.c.
- PostToolUse and PostToolUseFailure, matcher "*" (async): observation. The full tool_input and tool_response are JSON-serialised after `<private>` tag stripping and stored in SQLite (tool_uses table plus a queue). They go to the observer with fields capped at 16k chars, head/tail elided.
- Stop (async): summarize. SessionEnd (async): session-end.
- Worker: Bun HTTP server on 127.0.0.1:37700, SQLite DB under ~/.claude-mem, and Chroma started through uvx chroma-mcp. Search is hybrid FTS5 plus vectors.
- Observer: with provider claude and subscription auth, the Claude Agent SDK spawns the local `claude` binary with the user's OAuth login. - Its injected instructions push save_memory and work_state_write, competing with auto-memory and the task tools.
- claude-memory is fully redundant with auto-memory by its own README, and its hook is broken.
- claude-mem-cowork is mutually exclusive with claude-mem by design: inert while claude-mem is enabled, live (and cloud-bound) if claude-mem is disabled while cowork stays paired. Its skills (mem-search, agent-cost-report) duplicate claude-mem's.
- Notion memory connector: stores user and work context in Notion's cloud across clients. That is outside the stated trust boundary for evidence, but it is manual and opt-in per save, with no automatic capture of tool output. Auto-memory is the right home for project facts; neither Notion nor cmem.ai should hold evidence.
- Other evaluated tools: headroom (compression MCP and huge-file skill) overlaps claude-mem's smart_outline/smart_unfold "read less" tooling and its file-read gate philosophy. Running both means two layers deciding what file text the model sees.
- claude-code-setup and task-observer skills are unrelated.
- Hook stacking: claude-mem plus cowork both fire on PostToolUse, Stop, UserPromptSubmit and SessionStart, alongside any project hooks.
claude-mem.compatibility:
- Opus 5.5 at max effort: no model dependency. The observer is a separate Haiku 4.5 process (Sonnet for some tiers), billed to the same plan's 5-hour and weekly windows, competing directly with the Opus work.
- Ultracode/Workflow subagents: per code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks, plugin PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks fire inside subagents, carrying agent_id and agent_type.
  - claude-mem captures subagent tool events because SKIP_SUBAGENT_OBSERVATIONS=false. With batch size 1, that is one observer turn per subagent tool call, so cost scales with subagents × tool calls.
  - The file-read gate and SessionStart context skip subagents (agentId check; CONTEXT_MAIN_AGENT_ONLY=true). Whether the PreToolUse timeline injection also reaches subagents is unverified.
  - cowork would also rewrite every Agent/Task prompt and auto-allow it.
  - Skill and MCP listings are added to every subagent's context (observed in this subagent).
- Remote Control: no specific conflict found. The SessionStart systemMessage and hook-error notices would appear in the remote view. The local viewer (port 37700) is not reachable remotely, which is good.
- Current Bun-less state: sessions are NOT broken. The hooks fail fast (3–8 ms) as non-blocking errors and async hooks exit 1. Cost is noise in transcripts and a startup systemMessage pushing `npx claude-mem install`.
